precepts.text: Keep the words of the covenant and do them, that ye may prosper in all that ye do.
precepts.point: He rebels against the king of Assyria and smites the Philistines even unto Gaza.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

precepts.why:
“Keep therefore the words of this covenant, and do them, that ye may prosper in all that ye do.”

Hezekiah “clave to the Lord, and departed not from following him, but kept his commandments, which the Lord commanded Moses. And the Lord was with him; and he prospered whithersoever he went forth.”

Prospering here does not mean a mansion or luxury. It is the blessing that comes from keeping and doing the commandments: the Most High with him, rebelling against the king of Assyria and serving him not, and smiting the Philistines even unto Gaza.

precepts.text: The captivity comes because Israel would not hearken to the voice of the Most High.
precepts.point: The reason given again is that they obeyed not the voice of the Most High but transgressed His covenant and all Moses commanded.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

precepts.why:
The law says, “if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee.”

Samaria was besieged in Hezekiah’s fourth year and taken at the end of three years, and the king of Assyria carried Israel away into Halah, Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. Israel was carried away in stages, not all at once.

The reason is given again, in the words of the curse: “Because they obeyed not the voice of the Lord their God, but transgressed his covenant, and all that Moses the servant of the Lord commanded, and would not hear them, nor do them.” The captivity comes because Israel would not hearken.

moments.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell
Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time
The Pride Of Thine Heart Hath Deceived Thee!

points: Remember there were two kings; one king of Judah, the other king of Israel. Samaria was taken, and the king of Assyria did carry away Israel unto Assyria, because they obeyed not the voice of the Lord their God, but transgressed his covenant.

note.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell

points: Rabshakeh, the ambassador of the Assyrian army, spoke for the king to convince Judah to yield. Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah asked him to speak in the Syrian language, not in the Jews' language in the ears of the people on the wall. History note from class: the Assyrians and the Syrians were two distinct peoples whose languages intermingled; the Syrians are the children of Aram, Shemites, so Aramaic is Syrian, and through the migrations Aramaic slowly began to replace the paleo Hebrew we spoke.

note.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: Assyria was a rising empire conquering the nations around us. They destroyed the northern kingdom, then came against the southern kingdom during Hezekiah's reign. Hezekiah was a righteous king, so the Lord had his back, but Judah was very fearful.

note.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: Rabshakeh refused, and cried with a loud voice in the Jews' language so everyone would hear: let not Hezekiah deceive you; neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord, saying, the Lord will surely deliver us. Make an agreement with me, eat every man of his own vine, until I come and take you away to a land like your own land. Pay your tribute, and then I will deport you all out of your land and put our own people in it.

note.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: Have any of the gods of the nations delivered at all his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Their gods did not stop my king; yours will not either. But the people held their peace, for the king's commandment was, answer him not. Let him talk; do not say a word.

note.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: The first example of the punishment of the proud: the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh with a great host against Jerusalem, taunting king Hezekiah: what confidence is this wherein thou trustest? He mocked their trust in Egypt, a bruised reed, and mocked their trust in the Lord, and even claimed, the Lord said to me, Go up against this land, and destroy it.

note.label: The Pride Of Thine Heart Hath Deceived Thee!

points: He offered two thousand horses if they would give up, and threatened them with siege conditions in the crudest terms, and called out in the Jews' language so all the people on the wall could hear: let not Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord, saying, The Lord will surely deliver us. It is the same thing they try with us now: things get bad and the enemy says, you think your God is going to come and deliver you?

note.label: The Pride Of Thine Heart Hath Deceived Thee!

points: Make an agreement with me, and eat ye every man of his own vine: they threaten your resources, because they know once you cut off people's food and water, most will humble themselves and turn their back on God. That is why the bishop tells you to start putting food away.

note.label: The Pride Of Thine Heart Hath Deceived Thee!

points: Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered at all his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? He called out all the gods that could not stop him. But the people held their peace, and answered him not a word, for the king's commandment was, Answer him not. That is why the bishop says do not do interviews with these people; we do not have to answer them.

note.label: The Pride Of Thine Heart Hath Deceived Thee!

points: Hezekiah son of Ahaz begins to reign over Judah in the third year of Hoshea, the last king of Israel before the captivity.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: He does that which is right according to all that David his father did, removing the high places, breaking the images, and cutting down the groves.
He breaks in pieces the brazen serpent Moses made in the wilderness, which had stood from that time and was now being burned incense to, and he calls it Nehushtan.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Hezekiah trusts in the Most High so that none among the kings of Judah, before or after, was like him.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: He clave to the Most High, kept the commandments, and the Most High was with him so that he prospered.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: He rebels against the king of Assyria and smites the Philistines even unto Gaza.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: In Hezekiah's fourth year Shalmaneser besieges Samaria, and after three years, in Hezekiah's sixth year, Samaria is taken.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Israel was not removed all at once but carried away in stages into Assyria.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: The reason given again is that they obeyed not the voice of the Most High but transgressed His covenant and all Moses commanded.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Sennacherib king of Assyria comes up against the fenced cities of Judah and takes them.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Hezekiah sends to Lakish acknowledging offense and agrees to bear whatever tribute is laid on him.
Assyria appoints three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold, so Hezekiah gives all the silver of the house of the Most High and even cuts the gold from the temple doors.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: The king of Assyria sends Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh with a great host to Jerusalem, and they stand by the conduit of the upper pool.
He boasts that Assyria came up against the land by the word of the Most High Himself, claiming divine backing to destroy it.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Rabshakeh challenges Hezekiah's confidence, mocking his trust and calling Egypt a bruised reed that pierces the hand of any who lean on it.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: He argues that because Hezekiah removed the high places, even Judah's own worship is now confined to one altar, twisting the reform into a weakness.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah ask Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language so the people on the wall will not understand, but he refuses.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Rabshakeh cries aloud in the Jews' language, warning the people not to let Hezekiah deceive them or make them trust in the Most High.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: He promises the people their own vines, fig trees, and waters if they surrender, then a land like their own, seeking to turn them from their king.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: He asks whether the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah delivered their lands, claiming no god can deliver Jerusalem out of his hand.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: The people hold their peace and answer not a word, for Hezekiah had commanded silence.

note.label: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Threat

points: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah come to Hezekiah with their clothes rent and tell him the words of Rabshakeh.
